parts.name: Battery: 6S6P pack of Molicel P50B cells
parts.status: buy (36 cells, pack built by us)
parts.size: 36 Molicel P50B cells, each 21.7 mm wide × 70.4 mm tall, standing in a 6 × 6 block: 140 × 135 × 75 mm with nickel strip, BMS and wrap
parts.job: Powers the drone: an estimated 2.7 survey flights per charge. Six cells in series give 21.6 V under load; six in parallel give 30 Ah.
parts.why: 648 Wh in 2.72 kg. In a hot-day hover each cell carries 9.4 A, against a 60 A rating. It gives 58 min of loiter with 20 % left, or 2.7 survey flights per charge.
parts.instead: Samsung 50S ($6.99 a cell, $72 cheaper): voltage sag at our current not measured, so it needs a bench test first. Samsung 50E: 9.8 A rating, too low. A LiPo pack of the same mass would hold about 40 % less energy.
connects: XT90 connector, two 14 AWG wires per pole
calc: energy for one 15-minute survey, 1 km out and back
three flights, keeping the cells between 95 % and 10 % and 20 % in reserve
so the pack covers 2.7 flights, not 3; a 7P pack would fail the hover-thrust rule (Battery_Options)

parts.name: Power module: Holybro PM07
parts.job: Splits battery power to the five speed controllers and tells the flight controller the battery voltage and current.
parts.why: Rated 90 A continuous. Hot-day hover draws 57 A. Its stock 30 A input wire is replaced by two 14 AWG wires and an XT90.
parts.instead: PM08D (higher rating) if the wiring tests run hot.
connects: power and sensing cable (5 V, voltage, current)
calc: hot-day hover through the power module

parts.name: Servo regulator, 5–6 V, at least 5 A
buy: Key City Hobby (Castle Creations CC BEC 2.0)
parts.job: Powers the four servos from the battery.
parts.why: The ALPHA speed controllers have no built-in servo supply, so the servos need their own. Four servos at stall draw a few amps.
parts.instead: The Sky4 regulator, if its label shows 5 A or more.

parts.name: Lift motor: T-Motor MN5008 KV340
parts.job: Lifts the drone straight up for take-off and landing, and holds it in a hover.
parts.why: T-Motor's own test table for this motor with an 18 inch prop on 6 cells: 4.2 kg of thrust at full throttle. Our drone weighs 8.8 kg, so each motor carries 2,209 g in a hover, about 56% throttle at sea level and 65% on a hot day at 800 m. Total thrust is 1.55 times the weight on that hot day, above the 1.5 we require for control in gusts. Each motor draws 13.8 A in a hot hover and 33.5 A at full throttle, inside the 40 A speed controller.
parts.instead: The SunnySky V4014 motors we already own from Sky4: only 1.20 times the weight on a hot day, below the 1.5 rule.
parts.source: store.tmotor.com MN5008 test table (read 30 Oct); sheet 04 Lift_Hover
calc: thrust each motor holds in a hover
hot day at 800 m, from T-Motor's test table

parts.name: Lift propeller: T-Motor P18x6.1 (pair)
parts.job: Turns motor power into lift.
parts.why: This is the prop in the maker's MN5008 test, so the thrust numbers above apply directly.
calc: the maker's thrust figures are for this exact propeller

parts.name: Speed controller: T-Motor ALPHA 40A 6S
buy: United UAV (US stock, no import duty)
parts.job: Drives one lift motor at the speed the flight controller asks for. Sits in the boom nacelle next to its motor.
parts.why: Made for this motor class on 6 cells. Rated 40 A against 33.5 A at full throttle. The US price beats the China price once duty is paid.
parts.instead: Sky4's Tekko32: may work on 6 cells, model not yet checked. One four-in-one board would also put all four lift motors on one failure.
calc: full throttle, from the motor test table

parts.name: Pusher motor: T-Motor AT3520 KV550
parts.size: Ø 42 × 52 mm with the long shaft
parts.job: Pushes the drone forward once the wing carries it.
parts.why: Maker's test on 6 cells with a 13 inch prop: 3.6 kg static thrust at 34.9 A. In cruise we need 10.3 N; our estimate of the thrust left at 20 m/s is about 19 N, so level flight uses about half of it. Winged climb is limited, so we climb gently or on the rotors.
parts.source: store.tmotor.com AT3520 test table (read 17 Nov); sheet 04 Pusher

share of the pusher's thrust used in level flight (estimate)

parts.name: Pusher propeller: APC 12x6E
parts.job: Turns pusher power into forward thrust.
parts.why: Fits the tail with ground clearance. The 13 inch prop in the maker's test would leave only about 15 mm to the ground.

parts.name: Pusher speed controller: ALPHA 40A 6S
parts.job: Drives the pusher motor.
parts.why: Same part as the lift controllers; 34.9 A at full pusher throttle is inside its 40 A rating.

parts.name: Flight controller: Holybro Pixhawk 6C
parts.job: Flies the drone: reads the sensors, runs PX4's VTOL software, and commands the motors and servos.
parts.why: Owned, and PX4 supports quadplanes on it out of the box.
parts.instead: Our own flight-controller board is for Sky 3, not this drone.

parts.name: GPS and compass: Holybro M9N
parts.job: Position and heading.
parts.why: Owned. Mounted on the wing, away from the high-current wires that would disturb the compass.

parts.name: Airspeed sensor (Sky4)
parts.job: Measures airspeed so the flight controller knows when the wing can carry the drone and keeps it above stall.
parts.why: A quadplane needs it for transitions; we own one.

parts.name: Telemetry radio (Sky4)
parts.job: Two-way link to the ground station laptop.
parts.why: We fly within about 1 km, well inside its range.

parts.name: RC receiver (Sky4)
parts.job: Manual control link for the safety pilot.
parts.why: Owned, if Sky4 has one; otherwise a transmitter and receiver cost about $154.

parts.name: Remote ID: Ruko R111S
parts.job: Broadcasts the drone's identity and position, as the FAA requires.
parts.why: On the FAA's list of accepted Remote ID modules (RID000001939). Runs on its own battery, so it needs no wiring.

parts.name: Servo: KST X10 V2
parts.job: Moves the ailerons (roll) and the tail surfaces (pitch and yaw).
parts.why: 10 mm thin, so it fits inside the wing. 7.5 kg·cm at 6 V against 4.7 kg·cm needed in a 34 m/s dive.
parts.instead: KST DS145MG ($34.99): less margin and ships from China.
calc: aileron at a 34 m/s dive, with a factor of 2

parts.name: Wing: printed LW-ASA on carbon spars
parts.job: Carries the drone in forward flight. 2.24 m span, 0.50 m², SD7037 airfoil, 10° tips.
parts.why: Spar margin 1.52 at the root under 3.8 g with both lift motors at full thrust.
calc: stall speed with 0.50 m² and the SD7037 airfoil

parts.name: Booms: 30 mm carbon tubes with nacelles
parts.job: Hold the four lift motors, their speed controllers, the landing legs and the tail.
parts.why: Bending margin 1.97 in the hard-landing case; first bending mode 18–23 Hz, away from the rotor speeds.

parts.name: Fuselage: printed shell
parts.job: Holds the battery, the flight electronics and the payload.
parts.why: All parts fit with no overlaps in CAD.

parts.name: Arch tail
parts.job: Keeps the drone pointed into the wind and steady in pitch.
parts.why: Yaw stability Cnβ 0.139; all flight modes stable or slow enough for the autopilot.

parts.name: Payload computer: NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano
buy: Raspberry Pi 5, 4 GB (Adafruit), if a lighter logger is wanted
parts.job: Records every sensor with the time and position from the flight controller, and triggers the camera.
parts.why: We already own it. It takes the thermal camera over USB, the colour camera, the spot sensor and the air sensor over I2C, and reads position and time from the flight controller over a serial cable, so each reading is tagged with where the drone was. It draws 7 to 15 W.
parts.instead: Raspberry Pi 5 (4 GB, $130): about 130 g lighter and about 5 W less, enough for logging. Worth it if the hot-day hover margin gets tight.
parts.source: Jetson Orin Nano carrier board spec (DC input 9–20 V); payload_fit.py position

parts.name: Payload regulator: Pololu D36V50F12, 12 V 4.5 A
parts.job: Turns battery voltage into a steady 12 V for the payload computer.
parts.why: The battery runs from 25.2 V full to about 18 V empty; the Jetson accepts 9 to 20 V. This regulator takes 13.3 to 50 V in and gives up to 4.5 A at 12 V, about 3 times what the payload needs.
parts.instead: D36V50F5 (5 V, same price) if the Raspberry Pi 5 is used instead.

parts.name: Thermal camera: FLIR Lepton 3.5 on a PureThermal 3 board
parts.size: Lepton 11.8 × 12.7 × 7.2 mm on a 32 × 32 mm board, in a 40 × 30 × 22 mm printed case
parts.job: Measures the temperature of the shrub canopy, looking straight down.
parts.why: When chaparral shrubs run short of water they close their leaf pores and the leaves warm up compared with the air; leaf-minus-air temperature is a standard plant water-stress signal. 160 × 120 pixels, radiometric. At 60 m one pixel covers about 0.4 m, so a 1–3 m shrub spans several pixels. Its accuracy (about ±5 °C) is not enough alone, so warm and cool reference targets of known temperature sit in every flight.
parts.instead: FLIR Boson 320 or a Workswell WIRIS (thousands of dollars, asked by email). Same accuracy class as the Lepton without ground targets.
parts.source: Jackson et al. 1981 (crop water stress index); FLIR Lepton 3.5 datasheet; BEST_PRICES 10 Nov

parts.name: Colour camera: Raspberry Pi Global Shutter Camera, 6 mm lens
parts.size: 38 × 38 × 28 mm body, C/CS lens on top
buy: PiShop.us (camera $55, out of stock 18 Nov; lens about $25 not priced)
parts.job: Photographs the plot so we can find every shrub, see how much is plant and how much is bare soil, and build its 3D shape from overlapping photos.
parts.why: 1456 × 1088 pixels of 3.45 µm. With a 6 mm lens at 60 m one pixel is 3.5 cm and a photo covers 50 × 38 m, so 2 photos a second give 75 % overlap at 19 m/s, enough to build the canopy's 3D shape (photogrammetry). A global shutter takes the whole frame at once, so the picture does not skew at speed; 1 ms exposure smears 1.9 cm, under one pixel.
parts.instead: Livox Mid-360 lidar (265 g, 6.5 W): it looks sideways and up, and reaches only 40 m, so it cannot map the ground from 60 m. MAPIR Survey3W ($400) adds a near-infrared band.
parts.source: Raspberry Pi camera specs; Livox Mid-360 specs (read 18 Nov); our ground-resolution arithmetic

parts.name: 1610 nm spot sensor (built by us): two InGaAs photodiodes behind 1610 nm filters
parts.size: 50 × 40 × 45 mm printed head with a 20° view tube
parts.job: Measures how much 1610 nm short-wave infrared light the shrubs reflect, one reading per spot, plus the sunlight coming down.
parts.why: Water in leaves absorbs strongly near 1600 nm, so reflectance in this band drops as shrubs lose water; it is the standard leaf-water band. A camera for this band costs $5,650 or more (LUCID Triton SWIR) or rents for $2,250 a week, so for the first flights we build a two-channel sensor: one diode looks down through a 20° tube (a 21 m spot at 60 m), one looks up through a diffuser to read the sunlight. About $410 in parts plus $25 of small parts.
parts.instead: A SWIR camera through the companies we emailed (LUCID, Tech Imaging rental, SILIOS, Spectral Devices): images instead of spots, $2,250 a week to $30,000.
parts.source: Hunt and Rock 1989, Ceccato et al. 2001 (leaf water in the short-wave infrared); SPOT_SENSOR_CIRCUIT doc; prices BEST_PRICES 10 Nov

parts.name: Air temperature and humidity: Sensirion SHT45
parts.size: 25 × 18 mm board in a small printed sun shield
parts.job: Measures the air temperature and humidity at the drone, every flight.
parts.why: Leaf temperature only means stress when compared with the air around it and how dry that air is (vapour pressure deficit). ±0.1 °C and ±1 % humidity. It is checked against the ground weather meter in the shade before each flight.
parts.instead: Weather meter on the ground only: it misses the air at flight height.
parts.source: Adafruit SHT45 page (read 18 Nov); Idso et al. 1981
